content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents a method for training a GAN with a fully discrete latent space (instead of gaussian).
In doing so, the main challenge they face is encoding efficiency, that is how to scale the number of possible outputs in a discrete latent space of small size. The proposed solution, inspired by DNA, is to use a codebook from which they draw $n_g$ variants of genes of size $d_g$ that they concatenate to form the generative noise.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The idea is simple and effective.
- They get competitive results compared to the original continuous latents with both StyleGAN-2 and FastGAN backbones.

Weaknesses:
- The argument in Section 3.2 and its resolution is a little bit overplayed considering how simple the method is. I'm not convinced the parallel with DNA is helpful to understand the paper. It could even make it less clear overall.
- The results on the conditional tasks show that discrete latents could be usable in a downstream task, but the comparisons with the baselines are not convincing. In particular, the authors tune the temperature to obtain some good results, but a similar thing can be done with the baselines as well. Can the authors comment on the choice of temperature in Table 3 for the baselines?
- The paper struggle to find convincing motivation for the discrete embeddings.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written, even if the method is not delivered in the simplest manner.
The ideas are not novel, but the application and technical details are different enough from previous work.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I believe the main interest of the paper comes from the technical demonstration, that we can train competitive GANs with a fully discrete noise space fairly easily. Such a latent space would be easier to manipulate than a continuous one, and the experiments do indicate that the learned genome has some properties that could be taken advantage in some downstream task. Yet, I don't have a clear picture of what such a downstream task could be. It would help immensely if the authors could present one.

Meanwhile, I have to question the motivation and usefulness of the proposed method, as the novelty of the idea is insufficient to carry the submission by itself.

content.title: Response to Reviewer bh6L
content.comment:
We appreciate R.bh6L’s comments on the simplicity and effectiveness of our approach and its competitive results. We will try to address the reviewer's concerns:

**Weakness 1: Method’s simplicity and Section 3.2 argument**

We find the simplicity of our method to be an asset! One could easily substitute the continuous distribution with our genome and harness its benefits. In the main paper, we do so for StyleGAN2 and ProjectedGAN, and in the supplementary material for StyleGAN3 and 3d aware EG3D. 

In Section 3.2 we tried to both explain our method and lay the groundwork for our genome analysis. We find this is important as deriving the marginal attribute distribution for each gene and attribute, described in Section 3.3, is what permits us to turn our unconditionally trained model into a conditional generation method. The ability to do such an analysis is a trait of our proposed discrete codebook formulation. 
Regarding the DNA parallel, it is the initial motivation for this work. Interestingly, we found that, like its biological counterpart, our genome has specific genes that control the expression of certain attributes, as shown in Figure 2.

**Weakness 2: Unconvincing comparison with conditional/model. - Tuning the temperature of the baseline.**

We disagree with the premise of R.bh6L’s question. 

Firstly, note that our comparison to the baseline is not a fair one; the baseline can only generate the labels it was trained for. For StyleGenes, “we do not require a predefined number of classes and our method can be extended to more classes without training” as stated on page 8. Thus, our formulation does not just perform competitively but rather enables the creation of a conditional generative model out of an unconditional one.

Secondly, the conditional StyleGAN baseline does offer a straightforward way to use and fine-tune a temperature value.

Our method takes an unconditionally trained model, and with our discrete latent analysis, we enable conditional sampling from it. We do so by inferring by marginal attribute distribution for a given embedding variant as explained in Sections 3.3 and 4.2. Instead of sampling every variant uniformly, as done for the unconditional generation, we sample from the marginal distribution specific to the target attribute and each gene. We scale the distribution with the temperature value to increase the likelihood of sampling codebook entries with high probability. 

In contrast, the baseline is trained conditionally; it needs to have **all** the labels present both at train and test time. The conditional input to the model is a binary vector of all attributes: 1 denotes the existence and 0 the absence of each attribute. Thus, its formulation does not permit the use of a temperature value. To generate an image with (or without) the desired attribute, we set the attribute’s value to 1 (or 0). The rest are either (a) sampled randomly or (b) by using the pairwise statistics of the dataset. Specifically, if we want to generate a female face for each other attribute, e.g., long hair, we find the percentage of female FFHQ images that have long hair and use this number as the sampling probability of the long hair attribute. In Table 3, we denote the first approach (a) as “Sampling: random” and the second (b) as “Sampling: freq”.

**Weakness 3: Lack of convincing motivation for discrete embeddings.**

The discreteness of the latent space shows improved disentanglement and enables a straightforward analysis, as we show in Section 4.2. A lot of works tackle the analysis of StyleGAN’s continuous latent space. From our related works section: _“These approaches train a conditional normalizing flow (2) or a classifier (26) in the latent space to enable conditional sampling. In this study, we do not need to train a vector per transformation (15), compute any gradients(45) or apply clustering to hidden layers (8). In contrast, we treat the network as a black box and, without extra training, only harness the benefits of its discrete input to enable conditional generation.”_
Note that these approaches are orthogonal to our own. They can also be applied to our setting.

**Usefulness: What is the downstream task?**

As R.bh6L points out, our discrete latent space is easier to manipulate than a continuous one. This enables us to interpret better what effect each variant has on the synthesis output. We leverage this information **to turn our unconditionally trained model into a conditional one**. While we achieve competitive results to the conditionally trained baseline, we are not limited by a predefined set of conditional attributes. Our discrete analysis enables conditional sampling without the need to retrain or learn additional modules.

We see how this core contribution of our work could be made clearer for the readers in the introduction; we aim to highlight this in our revised manuscript version.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes StyleGenes, a method that replaces the continuous base distribution (e.g., uniform, Gaussian) in GANs with a discrete distribution over learnable embeddings from a codebook. A naive implementation of such a codebook would result in the number of parameters scaling linearly with the number of unique samples the model is able to generate. To address this issue, StyleGenes takes inspiration from the DNA and decomposes the latent vector into a set of "genes". Different genes can then be combined to drastically increase the number of distinct images the model can generate while keeping the parameter cost low. Experiments on unconditional and conditional image generation show that the model is able to improve the accuracy of conditional generation while being competitive on sample quality (measured by the FID). StyleGenes' latent codes are also better predictors of attributes in the generated image than StyleGAN suggesting a better disentanglement in the latent space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strengths]

- The paper is well-written and prior works have been sufficiently discussed.
- StyleGenes is a simple-to-implement method that works reasonably well. The proposed method improves the accuracy of conditional image generation compared to StyleGAN.

[Weaknesses]

- The major weakness of this work is its technical contribution and significance. The proposed method is a straightforward application of similarly explored ideas to the GAN framework. The key contribution --- replacing the base distribution in GANs with a discrete distribution over combinations of learnable embeddings --- is marginal. There are no surprises/significant contributions in the analysis and discussion either. While the authors have presented an interesting study, the overall contribution of this work is not significant enough.

content.title: Response to Reviewer teXc
content.comment:
We want to thank R.teXc for their response and for commending our writing, the completeness of our literature review, and how well it works while being easy to implement. Next, we aim to answer to the reviewer's questions.

**[Summary] - [Strengths]**

We find some core contributions of our work have been misinterpreted. Namely, R.teXc writes :

 _“The proposed method improves the accuracy of conditional image generation compared to StyleGAN.”_

Our comparison with StyleGAN is not a fair one. The baseline is trained conditionally; it needs to have **all** the labels present both at train and test time. The model can only generate the labels it was trained for. In contrast, our method takes an unconditionally trained model, and with our discrete latent analysis, we enable conditional sampling from it. As stated on page 8, “we do not require a predefined number of classes and our method can be extended to more classes without training”. Thus, our formulation does not just “improves the accuracy”, but rather enables the creation of a conditional generative model out of an unconditional one. We do so without any training for conditional sampling or retraining the model itself. 

We see how this core contribution of our work could be made clearer for the readers in the introduction; we aim to highlight this in our revised manuscript version.

**[Clarity]**

We thank R.teXc for their corrections and for commending our text.

**[Weaknesses] - [Quality] - [Novelty]**

We argue that it is not only that “the specific variant presented in this work is novel”, but rather without our formulation, the basic approach of discrete latents for GANs does not work. 

**“The proposed method is a straightforward application of similarly explored ideas to the GAN framework.” -  ”The proposed method is based on previously explored ideas of using a discrete distribution via a codebook as cited in the related works”**

While it is inarguable that we draw inspiration from Latent Code Quantization (LCQ), there are fundamental differences that set the two approaches apart:

- VQ-VAE[1]/GAN[2] codebook is learned through “...Vector Quantisation (VQ). The VQ objective uses the l_2 error to move the embedding vectors e_i towards the encoder outputs z_e(x)...” [1]. In our setting, there is no encoder. The codebook is trained through the adversarial game to produce realistic images. To our knowledge, this is the first work that can learn a discrete latent distribution in this manner.
- The discrete codes VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN learn are local descriptors spatially aligned in a grid. The models require a multitude of different codes to generate semantically rich and diverse images. In contrast, we generate images using a single code. Naively copying the LCQ approach as implemented in the above works would result in a codebook as large as the number of images we would like to generate.
- You need a lot of codes to generate an image. When they remove the encoder for inference, random local descriptors do not necessarily align well and thus require an extra model to help with the image sampling: VQ-VAE uses PixelCNN and VQ-GAN a transformer. However, we randomly sample arbitrary combinations during training and inference and only require a one-step approach, which renders our approach considerably faster.
- Our approach outperforms VQ-GAN on unconditional face generation on FFHQ

| Discrete Latent Models     | FFHQ 256 - FID |
|----------------------------|----------------|
| VQ-GAN                     | 9.6            |
| StyleGenes /w StyleGANv2   | 5.11           |
| StyleGenes /w ProjectedGAN | 4.19           |

**[Reproducibility] - [Questions]: Not providing code & Implementation details.**

We would like to refer to our Appendix B “Genome Codebase”. For the StyleGAN experiments, we **only** substitute the StyleMapping network with our Genome class. As we state on page 22: “We use the same arguments as the Mapping network to seamlessly substitute the function call”. Then the network is trained with the default configuration as described in our Experiments section on page 6.

[1] Neural Discrete Representation Learning by Aaron van den Oord, Oriol Vinyals, Koray Kavukcuoglu. NeurIPS 2017 -
[2] Taming Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis by Patrick Esser, Robin Rombach, Björn Ommer. CVPR 2021

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work builds on the general StyleGAN framework. Rather than using a continuous W space latent code for generation, this paper proposes to use a discrete codebook for representing the latent space. To avoid the increased computational cost of discrete embedding space, this work borrows the idea from the biology of DNA design by using a set of genes as basic components for composing the final latent code for the generation. The paper has conducted experiments comparing StyleGAN and ProjectedGAN for the quality of generation and disentanglement of latent space. Some experiments have also been conducted to demonstrate the generality and flexibility of the proposed algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

+ The idea of converting the continuous latent space into the discrete one itself is interesting. And the proposed idea of the inspiration from the biology DNA design should be useful if conducted properly.

+ The design of ablation studies for evaluating the different aspects of the model potential is thorough and appreciated.

+ Providing the code script is good for reimplementation and the full code with pertained models is encouraged to be released.

Weaknesses:

+ The motivation for using such a discrete space is not clear to me. The intro and abstract directly say that the paper aims to use another way by treating the latent space as discrete ones. After reading the whole paper, I am still not sure why such a method works for both visual quality and the disentanglement of latent code (if both of them have been evaluated properly). The paper justifies everything a little bit superficial without going deeper to gain more insights for the audience.

+ Using a discrete latent space for GAN to generate is not a novel idea though, which is also mentioned in the related work. For example, the well-known VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN demonstrated that using a discrete latent space can effectively save computational costs, especially for high-resolution images while achieving better visual quality. However, the paper selling the discrete space as the main contribution, without comparing any of such related works makes it hard to evaluate the contribution of this paper properly. Besides, the argument "without employing any encoder or self-supervised objective." seems inappropriate. It seems that this paper does train in an unsupervised way.

+ Could you please repeat how large the discrete space was used in the main experiments? How much computational burden has been introduced by the method? As the ability of disentanglement is the key advantage of StyleGAN, the way of evaluating in this paper seems vague. For example, what is the pertained classifier, and are they trained on certain latent space? Same as above, rather than simply saying that one method has a better performance. A much better way is to explain what causes such a case and the more insights, and these are the things that I believe contribute to the community the most. Besides, rather than showing the quantitative experiments, qualitative comparisons are also necessary as a generation result. Based on the visual examples, I am not confident about the disentangling ability of the proposed method, as many of the attributes have been adjusted together without preserving the identity of the input images.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 8rgR
content.comment:
We thank R.8rgR for appreciating our idea and commending our ablation studies for their thoroughness and the inclusion of our code; we plan to release the full code and pretrained models. We'll try to answer their questions:

**Weakness 1**: 
**Motivation on why discrete models vs continuous.**

The discreteness of the latent space shows improved disentanglement and enables a straightforward analysis, as we show in Section 4.2. A lot of works tackle the analysis of StyleGAN’s continuous latent space. From our related works section: “These approaches train a conditional normalizing flow (2) or a classifier (26) in the latent space to enable conditional sampling. In this study, we do not need to train a vector per transformation (15), compute any gradients(45) or apply clustering to hidden layers (8). In contrast, we treat the network as a black box and, without extra training, only harness the benefits of its discrete input to enable conditional generation.” 

Note that these approaches are orthogonal to our own. They can also be applied to our setting.

**Insights on disentanglement** 

We refer the reviewer to our analysis in Section 4.2 “Which genes are responsible for each attribute” and the accompanying Figures 2 and 11. There we see that for most attributes only specific genes are of importance. During training, each variant is sampled independently from the rest. We hypothesize that this pushes the variants to be semantically self-contained compared to the StyleMapping approach, which maps an undivided vector to the W space. This is supported by the results of our disentanglement studies. Note that we do so without sacrificing the visual quality of our results.

**Insights on visual quality**

Per our introduction, our method “includes the benefit of direct optimization of the samples” (of the distribution). Every variant of our genes is a learnable embedding. We do not assume a specific distribution, but our discrete latent distribution is trained through the adversarial game, as shown in Fig. 4. There we see the learned bimodal distribution for a gene on the Metfaces dataset. We find that the improvement of visual quality (FID) happens mainly in our ProjectedGAN experiments, where we substitute the Gaussian input. For the StyleGAN case, we substitute the StyleMapping network and observe a similar FID. StyleMapping is a push-forward transformation of a Gaussian prior to W space. We optimize our samples directly on the W space which, as our disentanglement studies show, improves the predictability of the output attributes from the latent code.

**Are the disentanglement and visual quality evaluated properly?**

We can see how our disentanglement studies can be confusing so please see our answer “Clarification on disentanglement studies”.
For our visual quality assessment, thanks to the StyleGAN3 codebase, measuring FID is easy and standardized. Similarly for ProjectedGAN. As we state in our experiments section, we run the experiments for the same number of iterations and hyperparameter settings. We report the best FID score for each method and dataset. 

**Weakness 2: Similarities to VQ-GAN**

While it is inarguable that we draw inspiration from Latent Code Quantization (LCQ) from VQ-GAN, there are fundamental differences that set the two approaches apart:
- VQ-VAE/GAN codebook is learned through “...Vector Quantisation (VQ). The VQ objective uses the l_2 error to move the embedding vectors e_i towards the encoder outputs z_e(x)...” [1]. In our setting, there is no encoder. The codebook is trained through the adversarial game to produce realistic images. To our knowledge, this is the first work that can learn a discrete latent distribution in this manner.
- The discrete codes VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN learn are local descriptors spatially aligned in a grid. The models require a multitude of different codes to generate semantically rich and diverse images. In contrast, we generate images using a single code. Naively copying the LCQ approach as implemented in the above works would result in a codebook as large as the number of images we would like to generate.
- VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN need a lot of codes to generate an image. In lack of an encoder, randomly sampled local descriptors do not necessarily align well, and thus require an extra model to help with the image sampling: VQ-VAE uses PixelCNN and VQ-GAN a transformer. However, we randomly sample arbitrary combinations during training and inference and only require a one-step approach, which renders our approach considerably faster.

Thus we find a comparison with these models is not apt. To summarize, our method is (1) self-learned and not quantized (using e.g., different losses and encoder). We do not believe that (2) moving from a single codebook, which would not work in our setting, to a compositional approach is trivial or insignificant. Our analysis shows how different design choices on the compositionality can vastly improve the expressibility of the codebook.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 8rgR (cont)
content.comment:
**Weakness 2: Similarities to VQ-GAN (cont)**

(3) Our method removes the need for an additional sampler, such as a transformer or PixelCNN.  Additionally, note that our approach outperforms VQ-GAN on unconditional face generation on FFHQ

| Discrete Latent Models     | FFHQ 256 - FID |
|----------------------------|----------------|
| VQ-GAN                     | 9.6            |
| StyleGenes /w StyleGANv2   | 5.11           |
| StyleGenes /w ProjectedGAN | 4.19           |

We would be more than open to suggestions for a fitting discrete latent-code baseline. 

**Weakness 3:**
**Size of Latent Space:** the output latent code has 512 parameters. The size of the codebook in terms of parameters equals “number of variants x 512”, regardless of the number of genes. We report the results of the experiments with the best FID score of our ablation studies. For FFHQ and Metfaces we use 2048 x 512 and for AFHQ 512 x 512. For Church and Bedrooms we only run the experiment with a codebook of size 2048 x 512. The recommended StyleGAN configuration uses two linear layers in the Mapping network, which results to 2 x 512 x 512 parameters. However, please consider the ablation study in Table 1. We observe only a small drop of FID with a codebook of 256 x 512 if we split our codebook into 64 smaller parts (= number of genes). This uses only 1/4 of the Mapping network’s parameters. As we discussed in Section 4.1, this is the most important takeaway of our approach: we can increase the performance without increasing the computational burden. 

**Clarification on disentanglement studies:** We can see how the reader can be confused by how this subsection is presented. We thank the reviewer, and we will address the issue. The pretrained classifiers refer to the same models we introduced in Section 4.2 page 7:

_“We pass each of these images through 40 pretrained CelebA classifiers ( 25 ). Their weights are included in the original StyleGAN ( 19 ) code repository, and we used the code provided by StyleSpace (45 ) to extract the logits for every image.”_

For the experiments, we sample 50.000 codes for StyleGAN, as produced by the StyleMapping network, and 50.000 codes for StyleGenes, a concatenation of randomly chosen variants for each gene. Then we use these latent codes to modulate the respective synthesis networks to produce 50.000 images from each, and we infer the existence of an attribute using the CelebA classifiers. We train a different MLP for each attribute that takes the latent code as input and predicts the presence of the attribute. The results are shown in Table 2, where we observe an average 10% increase in accuracy. 

We provide some insights on why this is happening in Supplementary Material (SM) A.1 “Evolution of StyleGenome during training” and the accompanying Figure 4 (page 13): 

_“As we discussed in Section 4.2, the StyleGAN’s ( 19 ) motivation to design the StyleMapping Network was to make the sampling density determined by the mapping and not to be limited to any fixed distribution; they aimed for the resulting space W to be more disentangled. In Figure 4 we can see how the adversarial game alters the density of our discrete distribution throughout the training. Our learnable embeddings are aligning, together with the Synthesis network, to better match the distribution of the real images”_

**Many of the attributes have been adjusted together without preserving the identity of the input images.**

We hypothesize that R.8rgR refers to our Image Manipulation experiment in SM A.3. and Figure 6. This is different from the aforementioned studies, where we claim that we improve the disentanglement abilities compared to StyleMapping, and not that we achieve perfect disentanglement.

Our manipulation approach shows an easy, yet coarse, way to manipulate generated samples by exploiting the discrete nature of our codebook. StyleGAN does not allow a similarly straightforward method. StyleGAN-based manipulation approaches, as discussed in our related works, require intricate methods and learning to perform the manipulation. These methods perform better and more disentangled manipulation and can also be applied to our method.

**Clarity, Quality, Novelty, and Reproducibility:**

We thank R.8rgR for their corrections and for commending our text.

Regarding our experiment’s “incompleteness”: In case our explanation above does not suffice, we would be thankful for any suggestions to address this incompleteness. 

Regarding the figures. We appreciate the feedback on our figures, and we will try to improve them. In Figure 1(b), the random z denotes that each variant is sampled uniformly for the unconditional case. This serves as a contrast to the conditional generation scheme of (c), where we use the marginal attribute distribution for a given embedding variant, as derived in Section 3.3. The thumbs up/down denote the presence/absence of an attribute. We will adjust the caption to make this clearer.

content.title: Response to Reviewer UdNg
content.comment:
We want to thank R.UdNg for their positive assessment. We appreciate the raised points and questions; they help us paint a clearer picture of our contribution! We will try to address their questions:

**Q1**: As R.UdNg mentions in their Q3, we use _samples_ to refer to the samples of the distribution. We draw a parallel to StyleMapping, where _samples_ from the Gaussian input are mapped to the W space. Similarly, we initialize the codebook with _samples_ from a gaussian distribution and optimize them directly in our W counterpart. They are optimized along the other network’s components through the adversarial game. Please refer to Figure 4, to see an example of how these samples evolve through training. 

**Q2**: The discreteness of the latent space shows improved disentanglement and enables a straightforward analysis (Section 4.2). Many related works tackle the analysis of StyleGAN’s continuous latent space. From Section 2: “These approaches train a conditional normalizing flow (2) or a classifier (26) in the latent space to enable conditional sampling. In this study, we do not need to train a vector per transformation (15), compute any gradients(45), or apply clustering to hidden layers (8). In contrast, we treat the network as a black box and, without extra training, only harness the benefits of its discrete input to enable conditional generation.” 
Note that these approaches are orthogonal to our own and can also be applied to our setting.
We also refer R.UdNg to our insights into disentanglement and visual quality, as described in our answer to R.8rgR. 

**Q3**: R.UdNg raises a great point. In our method, we have a non-learned categorical  
distribution that we sample uniformly from. Essentially, we learn its mapping to the continuous style space W through training. We do so by optimizing the corresponding embeddings of each discrete variant. We will make this clear in the text.

**Q4**: V_k is a vector of 512 elements: the concatenation of n_g smaller vectors for each gene, the variants. k is a vector of n_g indices. They dictate which variant we should use for each gene. After concatenation, v_k has the same shape as the output of StyleMapping.  

Thus, for the reviewer’s example with n_g = 64 and d=512, each variant is embedded in an 8-dimensional space, such as d /n_g = 8. We find that our PyTorch code on page 22 can also give some intuition to the process.

**Q5**: We use FID as a metric that incorporates both perceptual quality and variability. In our ablation studies, we fix d = 512 and find that (a) increasing the number of genes (= reducing the length of each variant) yields better performance. We get similar results when (b) we increase the number of variants for a fixed number of genes. We refer the reviewer to Table 1 - Right and section 4.1 “Unconditional generation” for our conclusion.

While we cannot claim that our method can elevate the mode collapse problem of unconditional GANs, our approach offers a powerful tool against mode collapse for conditional generation. As we state on page 8: “training conditionally with a small dataset can lead to poor performance and mode collapse (39)”. To generate conditionally, we only need our genome analysis as described in Section 3.3, without retraining our unconditional model or training any new modules.

**Q6**: We find this a great idea that we plan to explore in future work. However, note that even if we sample from the categorical distribution, the underlying values lie in a continuous space. Moreover, our experiments in interpolation and projection strongly indicate that our training formulation did not only learn how to translate our discrete samples into realistic images, it learned an underlying continuous distribution’s surface where our embeddings lie on. Thus, we think that our method is well-fitted for continuous data as well. 

**[Weakness] Not enough baselines.**

In the main paper, we compare two unconditional generation baseline models on 5 different datasets: StyleGAN2 and ProjectedGAN. The first uses StyleMapping for its continuous latent code, and the latter is a sampling from a Gaussian distribution. In Supplementary Material (SM), we show results using StyleGAN3 and the 3d-aware EG3D. For conditional generation, we compare with a conditional StyleGAN2 on FFHQ. Note that this comparison is not a fair one; the baseline can only generate the labels it was trained for. For StyleGenes, “we do not require a predefined number of classes and our method can be extended to more classes without training” as stated on page 8. Thus, our formulation does not just perform competitively but rather enables the creation of a conditional generative model out of an unconditional one. We are open to any baseline suggestions that would help elucidate the contribution of our method. 

**[Reproducibility]**
We include the StyleGenome code in the SM. We plan to release the code for the analysis and the pretrained models with the camera-ready version.

replying_to: Replying to StyleGenes: Discrete and Efficient Latent Distributions for GANs
